lessons.title: Penance, anointing, and the shape of conversion
lessons.explanation: Objective: describe the sacrament of penance and the anointing of the sick in their own structure, and distinguish the doctrine of sin from the assessment of any particular person's responsibility. Trent's fourteenth session describes the acts of the penitent — contrition, confession, and satisfaction — as, so to speak, the matter of the sacrament, required for its integrity and for the full remission of sins. Contrition is defined there as a sorrow of mind and a detestation for sin committed with the purpose of not sinning again; the tradition also distinguishes it from an imperfect sorrow, which it calls attrition. The same session teaches that the confession of sins was instituted by the Lord and is necessary by divine right for those who have fallen after baptism, that secret confession to a priest alone is not a human invention, and that the pastoral precept of annual confession comes from the Fourth Lateran Council — a discipline attached to a doctrine, not the doctrine itself. The effect of the sacrament is reconciliation with God and the Church. The seal, which binds the confessor to absolute secrecy, is treated in the Church's law and catechesis as inviolable. The anointing of the sick has a different history of interpretation. James 5:14–15 instructs the community to pray over and anoint the sick, and Trent's fourteenth session counts the anointing among the sacraments instituted by Christ. Sacrosanctum Concilium 73 then ordered the rite revised and the name changed so that it would be suited to the seriously ill rather than confined to the moment of death, and Paul VI's 1972 constitution Sacram Unctionem Infirmorum promulgated the revised rite. That reform is the clearest example in this level of a practice changing because of a renewed grasp of what the sacrament is for.
lessons.example: Consider a parish that advertises anointing only for the dying, on the stated grounds that the sacrament of the sick is the last sacrament of life. Trace the claim. James 5 does not restrict the practice to the dying; it speaks of the sick, with a promise of the Lord's support and the forgiveness of sins, and it situates the action in the community rather than at a deathbed alone. Sacrosanctum Concilium 73 extends the name and the purpose to those whose health is seriously impaired, and the revised rite that followed was designed for that wider use. So the parish's practice does not follow the Church's own intention, and the correction is not merely a matter of taste. Now consider a related confusion: viaticum, the reception of Communion as food for the journey, is indeed associated with the time of death, and the anointing may be repeated if a person's condition worsens or a new grave illness arises. The two actions are distinct, and a parish that collapses them loses the pastoral resource that the wider understanding was meant to provide. A further practical point: a chronic illness need not be terminal to warrant the sacrament, and the person's own request or a family's request can be brought to a priest without the family's having to decide that death is imminent.
lessons.question: A parish restricts the anointing of the sick to the dying on the ground that it is the final sacrament of life. What is the conciliar correction?
lessons.answer: Sacrosanctum Concilium 73 called for a revised rite and a changed name fitting the seriously ill rather than only the dying, and the 1972 revision enacted that intention.
lessons.distractor: The restriction is required, because the sacrament may be given only once and only at the point of death.
lessons.correction: The conciliar text says the anointing is for those whose health is seriously impaired, and the revised rite serves that purpose; it may be received again when illness recurs or worsens. Viaticum, Communion given near death, is a distinct act. The parish has confused a devotional assumption with the Church's own legislation.

depth.definitions: Contrition is sorrow for sin with the resolve to amend; attrition names an imperfect sorrow in the same direction, and the distinction does not license insincerity, since the sacrament requires the intention of amendment. Confession is the accusation of one's own sins to a priest; satisfaction is the penance performed in reparation. Mortal sin, in the Church's teaching, requires grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent; venial sin damages the relationship without severing it. The seal is the absolute obligation of the confessor to reveal nothing said in confession. Viaticum is the Eucharist given to a person in danger of death. Indulgences concern the temporal consequences of sin rather than the guilt that the sacrament removes. The term social sin, examined below, names a real phenomenon through an analogy that must be handled carefully.
depth.mechanism: The sacrament's structure explains both its severity and its mercy. A judgment about a person's acts requires that the acts be named; that is the rationale for confession, which the Church holds to be of divine institution rather than a convenient policy. A remedy requires that the sorrow be real; that is the rationale for contrition. Repair requires that harm be acknowledged; that is the rationale for satisfaction, which is a work of penance and not a payment for grace. The confessor's role is ministerial: he can judge the acts presented and the dispositions as they appear, and he cannot see into the interior of the person, which is why the Church forbids a teacher, a family member, or a curriculum from pronouncing on anyone's subjective guilt. Two failures sit on either side of this structure. Rigorism multiplies mortal sin and treats anxiety as evidence of seriousness. Laxity treats the sacrament as a mechanical erasure and ignores the requirement of amendment. The classically Catholic remedy for both is the same: the act, the intention, and the circumstances are examined honestly, the Church's teaching is consulted, and the assessment of an actual person's responsibility is left where it belongs. On indulgences, Trent's twenty-fifth session affirmed the Church's power to grant them and their usefulness while requiring that abuses be corrected, and the sixteenth-century controversy concerned both doctrine and the practical trade in them; a historical study of the abuses is a separate exercise from the doctrinal question, and neither replaces the other.
depth.secondExample: The concept of social sin illustrates the care a technical term needs. Reconciliatio et Paenitentia uses the phrase to name the way sinful choices accumulate in customs, structures, and institutions, while insisting on an analogy: sin in the strict sense is the act of a person, so structures cannot be absolved, cannot repent, and cannot be the subject of forgiveness. The practical consequence is double. An institution's failures cannot be reduced to individual bad actors, since the pattern is real and can be documented in policies, incentives, and omissions. But an institution cannot be the primary unit of conversion either, and a rhetoric that assigns blame to abstractions without asking anyone to change behaviour uses the concept to avoid the sacrament rather than to prepare for it. A congregation that discovers a systemic pattern of concealment should expect both: named persons taking responsibility, and structural changes adopted because individuals have repented. Confession offered as a substitute for institutional repair converts a sacrament of conversion into a procedural step; repair offered as a substitute for conversion converts a moral problem into an engineering one.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur and they are all errors of application rather than of doctrine. The first is using the three conditions for mortal sin as a diagnostic grid for judging other people. Those conditions describe what the Church's teaching requires for grave sin as a human act; whether they were met in a specific case is known to God and, imperfectly, to the person involved. A teacher who announces that a neighbour has committed mortal sin has stopped teaching and started pronouncing. The second is treating scruples as a mark of holiness; the ascetical tradition treats excessive anxiety about sin as a burden to be relieved rather than cultivated, and penance as a sacrament of peace. The third is treating indulgences as forgiveness of sin, when the doctrine locates them in the removal of temporal consequences, and treating the requirement of confession as a merely ecclesiastical formality, when the Church's teaching says otherwise. Each error has a practical diagnostic: ask what the claim presupposes that the speaker could actually know.
depth.application: Optional practice: prepare a structured examination of conscience for an adult who has asked for one, using the pattern of the commandments together with the duties of that person's own state of life. The model should be a framework, not a script: for each area, what the person owes, what the ordinary failure looks like, and what repair would involve, including restitution where property or reputation was harmed. Then address two invented cases. In the first, a scrupulous person asks how often they should confess a habitual fault; the model distinguishes the gravity of the act, the disposition of the person, and the pastoral guidance a confessor would give, and declines to set a rule for someone it has never met. In the second, a person with a chronic illness asks whether they may be anointed before a surgery that is not expected to be fatal; the model points to the Church's revised understanding of the sacrament for the seriously ill and refers the decision to the person's pastor. Self-review rubric: restitution named where harm occurred; no claim to assess anyone's interior state; no personal medical or confessional information recorded anywhere in the exercise.
depth.summary: Penance is a judgment and a remedy at once, structured around contrition, confession, satisfaction, and absolution in the Church's custody, while anointing is a sacrament of the seriously ill whose modern form reflects a recovered understanding of its purpose. Neither can be operated by a teacher on another person's conscience. The next lesson takes up the reasoning a person does before and around such decisions: conscience and moral judgment.

lessons.title: Conscience and moral reasoning: judgment, formation, and the moral act
lessons.explanation: Objective: explain conscience as an act of practical judgment, show how a moral act is analysed, and distinguish which parts of a moral dispute are settled teaching and which are prudential or contested. Gaudium et Spes 16 describes conscience as the most secret core and sanctuary of a person, where the law written by God is heard, and calls fidelity to conscience the dignity of the human person. The same council's declaration on religious freedom treats freedom of conscience as immunity from coercion, including for those who do not fulfil the duty of seeking religious truth. Two things follow at once. Conscience is not a feeling; it is a judgment of reason about what is to be done here and now. And because it is a judgment, it can be correct or mistaken, informed or neglected, which is why the Church's teaching insists on formation as well as on liberty. Veritatis Splendor examines the structure of the moral act, and its numbered sections are the ones to read: section 65 addresses the influential theory of a fundamental option, a deep self-determination held to be separable from particular choices, and the encyclical rejects the separation while accepting that a person's moral life has an orientation deeper than isolated acts. Section 75 discusses teleological and consequentialist theories that weigh pre-moral goods to determine rightness. Section 78 identifies the object of the act as what the agent chooses, and section 80 argues that negative precepts forbidding certain kinds of action admit no exceptions, because the object itself is disordered. This teaching is authoritative papal teaching; it is not presented as an infallible definition, and Catholic theologians have argued about it — some before and after its publication defended versions of the theories it rejects. Stating that plainly belongs to reading accurately: the encyclical's position is the Church's, and disagreement with it is a real position rather than an unrecognised one.
lessons.example: Work through a case with no doctrinal ambiguity and no easy escape. A manager is asked to sign a report that omits a material risk which, if disclosed, would delay a project on which the manager's own bonus depends. First, name the object: the act is not merely signing a document but presenting a document as complete when it is not, which is an act of deception about a matter affecting investors and colleagues. Second, the intention: the manager wants the project to proceed and wants the bonus. The intention does not change the object, though it explains how the temptation is experienced. Third, the circumstances: the information is available, the omission is deliberate, and the affected parties include people who will bear losses that disclosure would have prevented. Now consult the sources: this belongs to the field of the eighth commandment and of the Church's teaching on truthfulness and on the duties of those who administer property. The analysis reaches a conclusion without psychology. Notice what the case does not require: no claim about the manager's eternal state, no calculation of consequences that could license the omission because the project's benefits were large enough, and no assumption that the manager's sincerity settles anything. Sincerity is a feeling; the act is what was done. If instead the report flagged the risk in a footnote nobody read, the object changes, and the analysis turns on whether disclosure was genuine — a factual question about the document rather than a moral disagreement about principle.
lessons.question: A person says: “My conscience tells me this is right, so no further inquiry is needed.” What is the Catholic response?
lessons.answer: A certain conscience must be followed, but the duty to form conscience remains, so an unexamined judgment may be a culpably unformed one rather than a verdict to be honoured.
lessons.distractor: The claim is correct, because the individual conscience creates moral truth for that person.
lessons.correction: The tradition holds both that a person must not act against a certain conscience and that conscience must be formed by Scripture, by the Church's teaching, by counsel, and by reflection on experience. Freedom from coercion, which the council's declaration on religious freedom affirms, is not a licence to skip inquiry; the same document affirms the obligation to seek the truth.

depth.definitions: Conscience here is a practical judgment of reason, not a sentiment and not a separate faculty of revelation. The moral act has three components: the object, meaning what the agent chooses to do considered as a kind of action; the intention, meaning the end for which it is done; and the circumstances, meaning the surrounding particulars. An intrinsically evil act is one whose object is disordered regardless of consequences. Prudence is the practical virtue of deciding well in particular circumstances. An erroneous conscience holds a mistaken judgment; vincible ignorance is culpable and could reasonably have been corrected; invincible ignorance, in the traditional account, could not. The fundamental option names the theory that a deep self-determination is separable from particular choices. Consequentialism judges acts by outcomes, and proportionalism weighs pre-moral values against one another.
depth.mechanism: The three components operate in an order that is easy to state and hard to apply. The object has priority: if the kind of act is disordered, good intentions and pressing circumstances cannot repair it in the encyclical's account, though they may affect the agent's guilt and the gravity of the case. The intention can change the moral character of a wider plan — giving a gift to reconcile with an estranged friend is not bribery — but it cannot turn deceit into truthfulness. Circumstances can aggravate or mitigate, and they matter practically because they are the material of prudence. The classical principles about erroneous conscience are the pastoral complement: a person must not act against a judgment they are certain of, even when the judgment is wrong, because to act against one's practical reason is to act against what one currently takes to be right; an uncertain judgment must be resolved before acting; and ignorance diminishes responsibility to the extent that it was not culpable. Applying this to a third party is impossible in the way people imagine. A teacher can analyse acts, cite teaching, and identify what evidence would bear on a decision. A teacher cannot pronounce on another person's culpability, because that depends on knowledge and freedom no observer can inspect. That limit is not evasion; it is a claim about what moral knowledge is available.
depth.secondExample: Take the classical case of a mistaken conscience, adapted. A nurse is convinced, on grounds the Church rejects, that a particular procedure is morally required in a case at hand, and the hospital's policy forbids it. Several distinct questions hide inside the situation. Is the nurse's judgment actually mistaken? If so, was the mistake a matter of accessible information a reasonable person would have found? What does the Church's teaching say about the act itself? And what may the institution do about a demand that conflicts with its own commitments? Conflating them produces a slogan on either side. “Conscience is absolute” treats an unformed judgment as a verdict others must accommodate. “Just follow the rule” treats the genuine difficulty of a person unable to act against a settled conviction as though it were stubbornness. The tradition's own vocabulary — certain versus doubtful conscience, vincible versus invincible ignorance, and the distinction between what the act is and what the agent knew — was developed precisely to keep these questions apart, and it remains more useful than either slogan.
depth.mistake: Four mistakes recur. Equating conscience with feeling, which makes moral inquiry redundant because nobody can be argued out of a feeling. Treating conscience as irrelevant once a rule exists, which is the opposite error and makes prudence pointless; the tradition's long practice of casuistry exists because applying a principle to particulars is an art. Reading a genuine theological controversy as permission to disregard the teaching: a theologian's argument against a section of an encyclical is an argument inside the Catholic conversation, not a licence for a seminar to treat the teaching as optional. And mistaking the consequences of an act for its evaluation, so that a large enough benefit is imagined to sanctify a disordered means — the exact move that section 80 excludes for the acts it discusses.
depth.application: Optional practice: analyse three invented cases — a journalist deciding whether to publish a name, a student deciding whether to reuse an unattributed passage, and a supervisor deciding whether to report a safety defect — using a fixed four-step structure: state the object, the intention, and the salient circumstances; identify the relevant teaching and cite it; identify the facts still needed; identify which part of the judgment is settled by teaching and which is prudential. Model entry for the third case: the object is the act of reporting or concealing a known danger; intention and circumstances shape severity; the relevant teaching concerns truthfulness and the duties of office; the open facts concern whether the danger is genuine and already known; the prudential judgment concerns how and when to report. Self-review rubric: the object separated from the intention; at least one citation from an assigned source; no verdict on any person's culpability; a clearly marked line between settled teaching and practical judgment.
depth.summary: Conscience is practical reasoning that can be formed or neglected, and the moral act is analysed by object, intention, and circumstances rather than by outcomes alone. The Church's teaching is authoritative and also the subject of live theological argument, which is a fact to report rather than conceal. The final lesson turns to the company in which a Catholic moral life is lived: the communion of saints, and the devotion that has grown around Mary.

lessons.title: The communion of saints: Mary, the saints, and what devotion does and does not claim
lessons.explanation: Objective: state what the Church teaches about the communion of saints and Marian devotion, and sort the practice into doctrine, theological explanation, and legitimate or illegitimate piety. The creed's phrase refers to the Church as a communion, and the Catechism explains it in two linked senses, given at paragraphs 946–962: a sharing in holy things, and a communion among holy persons. Lumen Gentium 48–51 develops the second sense, describing one Church in three states — the pilgrim community on earth, those being purified, and the glorified — joined by charity in a single communion in which prayer and intercession flow between them. The Council of Trent's twenty-fifth session then teaches that the saints reigning with Christ offer their own prayers to God for people, that it is good and useful to invoke them suppliantly, and that this benefits those who ask — while adding that all of it is asked through Christ, “who is our alone Redeemer and Saviour.” That clause is the doctrinal guardrail. Veneration is not worship: the tradition's vocabulary distinguishes latria as the worship owed to God alone, dulia as the veneration of the saints, and hyperdulia as the higher veneration given to Mary — a theological vocabulary rather than a conciliar formula, but one that expresses the same boundary Trent drew. Mary's standing rests on titles that are taught rather than merely felt: Lumen Gentium 53 calls her truly the Mother of God and Mother of the Redeemer, and immediately notes that she was redeemed by reason of her Son's merits. Lumen Gentium 62 uses the title Mediatrix and then limits it in the same sentence: this is to be so understood that it neither takes away from nor adds anything to the dignity and efficaciousness of Christ the one Mediator.
lessons.example: A parish leaflet announces a novena with a promise: recite these prayers for nine days and your request will be granted. Audit it in three steps. First, what does the Church claim about intercession? Trent XXV: the saints pray for people, and invoking them is good and useful. It claims a request and a benefit, not a lever. Second, does anything oblige God to grant a particular outcome? Nothing in the sources does, and the point is not pedantic: treating a prayer as a mechanism converts a relationship into a technology, which is the very confusion the veneration vocabulary exists to prevent. Marialis Cultus 38 names two deviations the Council reprobated — an exaggeration of content and form that falsifies doctrine, and a small-mindedness that obscures Mary's figure and mission — and it lists among the faulty attitudes a vain credulity that substitutes reliance on external practices for serious commitment, and a sentimentality alien to the Gospel's demand for persevering action. The leaflet fails on the first. Now consider the opposite correction: an editor who strips the novena of every request because petitions to saints are unbiblical. That over-corrects. A revised leaflet would ask the saints to pray for the intention, name the persons or needs involved, and add that the outcome is entrusted to God's will with a concrete act of charity attached — which is exactly what the Church's own documents ask of popular piety.
lessons.question: A catechist says Mary's cooperation adds something to Christ's saving work. What correction does Lumen Gentium 62 supply?
lessons.answer: The council uses the title Mediatrix only with the express qualification that it neither takes away from nor adds anything to the dignity and efficaciousness of Christ, the one Mediator.
lessons.distractor: The statement is sound, because Mary's cooperation completes what Christ's work left unfinished.
lessons.correction: That last phrase is precisely what Catholic teaching denies. Mary's role is presented as a participation in and a service of Christ's mediation, not an addition to it; the council's wording exists to exclude the very inference the catechist drew. Her own words in Luke 1:46–55 are those of a servant who praises what God has done.

depth.definitions: The communion of saints names the shared life of the Church, understood in two senses: communion in holy things, and communion among holy persons. The three states are the pilgrim Church on earth, those undergoing purification, and the glorified. Intercession is prayer on behalf of another; invocation is the request that the saints intercede. Latria is worship owed to God alone; dulia is the veneration of saints; hyperdulia is the higher veneration of Mary. Canonisation is a definitive declaration that a person is in glory — the doctrinal commentary on the profession of faith lists it among what it calls dogmatic facts. Popular piety is the devotional practice of a people, which the Church regulates and encourages within limits. The treasury of merit is the theological account of the Church's shared spiritual goods, which also underlies the doctrine of indulgences.
depth.mechanism: The argument for intercession is ecclesiological rather than empirical. Catholic teaching holds that the Church is one body whose members are not separated by death, so that prayer within the body can be addressed to its glorified members without dividing the body's dependence on Christ. What the sources do not claim is that the saints act on their own authority, that they know everything, or that a request obliges God. Catholic theology typically explains how the glorified can be aware of petitions by their share in God's knowledge, and that explanation is theology rather than defined doctrine — worth saying plainly, because devotion often assumes more than the Church teaches. Two practical consequences follow. Because the practice rests on the communion of the Church rather than on a demonstration available to any observer, a Catholic should be able to present it as a theological commitment, not as a neutral finding; and because the practice involves requests for help, it is especially vulnerable to creeping magic, which is why the Church's documents regulate popular piety rather than merely tolerating it. The directory on popular piety is the practical counterpart to the doctrinal texts: it approves practices while requiring that they serve the liturgy and the Gospel rather than compete with them.
depth.secondExample: Relics make the boundary concrete. Trent's twenty-fifth session teaches that honour is paid to the relics of saints, and it gives the reason: the bodies of the saints, which were living members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit, will be raised in glory. The same decree rejects the notion that any divinity or virtue resides in images on account of which they are to be worshipped or from which anything is to be asked, and it grounds the honour in the relation of the sign to what it represents. Now take a parish that advertises a relic's presence with the claim that a donation will bring a financial blessing. The second half of that sentence has abandoned the structure the decree sets up: honour is directed through the sign, and nothing is to be asked of the object. A corrected announcement would describe the relic, explain the veneration offered, place the celebration within the liturgy, and ask for prayer rather than for an expected return. The case is useful because the abuse and the practice share a surface: both involve an object and a crowd. Only the doxology — who is being honoured, and who is being asked — distinguishes them, which is why getting that distinction right is not pedantry but the whole practice.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The charge that Catholics worship Mary, which the veneration vocabulary exists to answer, and which a careless Catholic can inadvertently confirm by language that treats her as a source of grace. The assumption that the saints function independently of God, corrected by Trent's own clause that Christ is our alone Redeemer and Saviour. The opposite error of dismissing popular piety wholesale — Lumen Gentium 67 warns against both gross exaggeration and petty narrow-mindedness about Mary's dignity, so a lesson that only polices excess has taught half of the Church's position. And the assumption that the practice of asking the dead to pray for us is either a neutral historical finding or a superstition to be refuted; it is a theological practice whose premises can be stated, examined, and disagreed with, and honest teaching states them. Other Christian traditions honour Mary while rejecting the invocation of saints and the two modern definitions; the Orthodox churches venerate Mary and the saints while not receiving those definitions as they stand. A Catholic presentation that cannot describe those positions accurately has not understood its own.
depth.application: Optional capstone: audit a devotional leaflet of your own composition, then revise three sentences. Sentence one: a promise of a guaranteed outcome. Sentence two: a request for a material benefit made to an image or object. Sentence three: language that treats Mary or a saint as an independent source of grace. For each, write the corrected version using one of this lesson's sources as the reason: Lumen Gentium 62 for the mediation limitation, Trent XXV for the object of honour and the ground of invocation, Marialis Cultus 38 for the two deviations. Model correction for sentence one: the novena asks the intercession of the saint for a specific intention, with the outcome entrusted to God's will, and includes an act of charity as part of the practice. Self-review rubric: every correction tied to a source with a locator; the doxological direction of each sentence stated; at least one legitimate devotional practice retained and explained rather than amputated, to show that the audit distinguishes excess from ordinary piety.
depth.summary: The communion of saints is a claim about one Church across death, expressed in an intercession that asks rather than commands, and guarded by a vocabulary that reserves worship for God alone. Mary's titles are taught and their limits are taught with them, and the Church polices exaggeration and contempt simultaneously. That completes this level's movement from how doctrine is defined and read, through grace and the sacraments, to the moral life and the company it is lived in.

readings.title: Council of Trent, Session XXV: on the invocation and veneration of saints, relics, and sacred images
readings.note: Read the passage teaching that the saints pray for people and that invoking them is good and useful, and the clause that Christ is our alone Redeemer and Saviour; then read the sentences on images and what is not to be asked of them. Public-domain 1848 translation hosted for study, not an official Holy See edition.

readings.title: Lumen Gentium 48–51, 62, 67
readings.note: Read 48–51 for the three states and the communion of the pilgrim Church with the glorified, 62 for the Mediatrix title and its immediate limitation, and 67 for the warnings against exaggeration and narrow-mindedness. Conciliar text; section numbers locate each claim.

readings.title: Marialis Cultus 38 (Paul VI, 1974)
readings.note: Read the section listing faulty attitudes in Marian devotion — vain credulity and sentimentality among them — and the Council's reprobation of exaggeration and narrow-mindedness. An apostolic exhortation: pastoral and normative, not definitional.

readings.title: Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy (Congregation for Divine Worship, 2001), chapter V, nn. 183–207
readings.note: Read the principles for Marian devotion and then sample the recommended practices, noting that the directory's purpose is to order popular piety around the liturgy rather than to replace it. A dicastery instruction, so its norms are disciplinary as well as doctrinal.

readings.title: ARCIC, Mary: Grace and Hope in Christ (2005)
readings.note: Read the commission's account of what Anglicans and Catholics can affirm together about Mary and where the commissions records remaining difference. An agreed statement of a dialogue commission hosted by the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, not an act of the magisterium.

visual.title: Who is being addressed, and how?
visual.description: A three-column frame that classifies a devotional practice by its object, its verb, and its ground.
steps: Object: God, a saint, or an image or object?
Verb: worship, venerate, ask to intercede, or expect an effect from the thing?
Ground: which source supports the practice, and what does that source claim?
Limit: what does the practice not claim about Mary, the saints, or God's obligation?
Correction: if the practice fails, what is retained and what is amended?

questions.prompt: One speaker says Trent teaches that people earn justification by good works, and another says that because grace does everything, conduct cannot affect a believer's standing. Which correction addresses both?
questions.answer: The decree presents grace as prevenient and merit as itself grounded in grace, while its canons also reject presumption about one's predestination and the claim that nothing further is required.
questions.distractor: Both statements are accurate, because Catholic teaching deliberately holds incompatible positions in tension without resolution.
questions.correction: Trent denies that justification is earned and denies that it leaves the person unchanged. Its canons on assurance and predestination cut against the second speaker, and its account of prevenient grace cuts against the first. Gift and responsibility are held together, not balanced against each other.

questions.prompt: An adult baptised as an infant in another Christian community asks a Catholic parish to be baptised again “properly.” What is the correct pastoral and doctrinal response?
questions.answer: Recognise the Baptism if it used water and the Trinitarian formula, do not repeat it, and prepare the person for reception into full communion, reserving an inquiry into validity for genuine doubt.
questions.distractor: Baptise the person again, since Baptism outside the Catholic Church conferred nothing.
questions.correction: Trent's seventh session teaches that Baptism imprints an indelible character, which is why it is not repeated, and Catholic practice recognises a Baptism conferred with water and the Trinitarian formula. Where doubt about form, matter, or intention exists, the doubt is investigated — the remedy for ambiguity is evidence, not repetition.

questions.prompt: A priest publishes a blog post recounting, in identifying detail, what a penitent confessed, arguing that the penitent's conduct had already become public. What is at stake?
questions.answer: The seal of confession is inviolable: what is said in confession may not be revealed, and publishing identifying details of a penitent's sins compounds the violation regardless of motive.
questions.distractor: The seal is a disciplinary courtesy that lapses when a penitent's conduct is already known to others.
questions.correction: The seal is treated in the Church's law and in the Catechism as absolute, and it does not depend on the secrecy of the underlying facts. A public reputation may be discussed in general terms by anyone; the content of a confession is not available for that discussion at all — which is also why confessional and personal information should never enter a course exercise.

questions.prompt: After a public scandal, a commentator states that the person involved certainly committed a mortal sin. What is the methodological problem?
questions.answer: Mortal sin as the Church teaches it requires grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent, and no outside observer has access to the last two.
questions.distractor: Mortal sin is determined by the gravity of the external act alone, so any public scandal proves it.
questions.correction: The conditions describe what the Church's teaching requires for grave sin as a human act; they are not a diagnostic instrument for third parties. The commentator has converted a moral analysis into a verdict about another person's interior state, which is exactly the move this level's earlier lessons refuse.

questions.prompt: A leaflet advertises a novena with a guaranteed outcome and invites donations in the presence of a devotional image, promising a return. Which correction follows the sources?
questions.answer: The novena may ask the saint's intercession for a stated intention, with the outcome entrusted to God, and honour is directed to God; nothing is to be asked of an image or object.
questions.distractor: Popular piety lies outside the Church's regulation, so the leaflet stands as written.
questions.correction: Trent's twenty-fifth session grounds invocation in the saints' prayers and denies that any divinity or virtue in an image is to be venerated, Lumen Gentium 62 limits mediation, and Marialis Cultus 38 names vain credulity among the faulty attitudes the Council reprobated. The directory on popular piety exists because the Church regulates rather than merely tolerates these practices.

questions.prompt: A news report says a pope “declared” a contested policy position to be Catholic doctrine, and the report's verb is quoted onward by three commentators. The underlying act turns out to be a letter explaining a revision to a paragraph of the Catechism. Describe the correction a careful reader should make to the report, and describe what the letter itself claims.
questions.answer: Locate the act — a dicastery letter explaining a revised Catechism paragraph — classify it as an explanation arguing for continuity with prior teaching rather than a new definition, and assess the argument for continuity on its merits.
questions.distractor: Accept the report's verb, since a papal act of any genre carries the highest level of authority and the argument for continuity is therefore settled in advance.
questions.correction: The verb in the report is the journalist's summary, not the document's modality. Donum Veritatis 24 lists nature of document, insistence, and manner of expression as the criteria. The lesson's method then asks whether the letter's continuity argument holds, which is a question the letter's own claim does not answer for the reader.

questions.prompt: A homilist reads from a Catholic Study Bible and builds a doctrinal claim on a sentence that appears in the editorial footnote beneath the passage rather than in the sacred text itself. A listener, reading along, cannot find the sentence in a different edition. Explain what has gone wrong and what the doctrinal claim would need instead.
questions.answer: The footnote is scholarly annotation with its own authorship, not the inspired text; the doctrinal claim needs a located source in Scripture, the Church's teaching, or a cited document.
questions.distractor: Footnotes carry the same authority as the verses because they are printed by the publisher of the Bible.
questions.correction: The distinction is between the sacred text, the Church's living interpretation of it, and a scholar's or editor's note. A study Bible's notes serve readers and may be excellent, but citing them as Scripture confuses three different kinds of authority — the same confusion the reading method in this level is designed to prevent.

questions.prompt: A community introduces a changed practice and defends it on the ground that “the Church's doctrine develops, so our practice is apostolic,” while also treating a rule about the celebration as though it were irreversible doctrine. Identify both errors and state what the defence actually requires.
questions.answer: A development claim is an argument requiring earlier and later propositions plus a stated bridge, while a disciplinary rule may simply be changed by competent authority; neither a change of practice nor an assertion of development establishes apostolic origin.
questions.distractor: The defence is sound because any practice that arises after a doctrinal development inherits apostolic authority from that development.
questions.correction: Development concerns understanding of the deposit; discipline concerns rules that can be revised without any change of doctrine. The community has asked a development argument to do the work of evidence, and at the same time has asked a rule to do the work of a dogma — which is the two-sided error this level's first lesson described.

questions.prompt: A pamphlet states that the title Coredemptrix is now dogma because a pope used the word in a homily and a petition has been signed by many bishops. A reader asks what would be required for the claim to be true, and what status the title actually has.
questions.answer: A papal homily and a petition do not define anything; a dogma requires an act proposing a revealed truth for belief, and no such act has defined this title, which remains a matter of theological discussion and devotional usage.
questions.distractor: Widespread use by bishops and popes converts a title into dogma, so the pamphlet is describing a completed act.
questions.correction: The first category in the classification scheme requires a truth divinely revealed and proposed as such, whether by solemn definition or by the ordinary and universal magisterium. Frequency of usage is not one of the criteria; and the council's own use of the related title Mediatrix carries an explicit limitation (Lumen Gentium 62) which a maximalist reading ignores.

questions.prompt: A discussion group concludes from the doctrine of justification by grace that confessing sins is a leftover of a pre-Reformation mentality, and that a person who repents privately need never approach the sacrament. Which sources answer the conclusion, and what do they say?
questions.answer: Trent's decree on justification presents grace as gift while requiring a change of life, and its decree on penance teaches confession of sins after baptism as instituted by the Lord and necessary by divine right, with contrition, confession, and satisfaction as the acts of the penitent.
questions.distractor: The group is right, because a sacrament that involves enumeration of sins contradicts the gratuity of grace.
questions.correction: Gratuity and remedy are not competitors. The doctrine of grace denies that the sacrament is a payment; the doctrine of penance supplies the remedy the same tradition says the baptised need. The group has imported a false antithesis, and the ecumenical documents on justification do not support it either — the Joint Declaration explicitly leaves open questions about the sacramental life.

questions.prompt: A catechist explains that Baptism imprints an indelible character and concludes that a baptised person's later conduct cannot affect their standing before God, adding that Paul's moral commands in Romans 6 are directed only to the unbaptised. Assess both claims.
questions.answer: The character doctrine explains why Baptism is not repeated, not moral immunity; Paul's commands in Romans 6 are addressed to the baptised and specify the conduct fitting the new life they have received.
questions.distractor: The character guarantees perseverance, and Romans 6 therefore describes the condition of those who have not yet received the sacrament.
questions.correction: Two distinct doctrines have been merged. The character concerns the sacrament's non-repetition; the moral life concerns a continuing relationship that Paul's imperatives presuppose in their addressees. Sacrosanctum Concilium 59 adds that sacraments both presuppose and nourish faith, which is incompatible with the claim that reception makes formation unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A student defends ignoring the encyclical's teaching on intrinsically evil acts by noting that well-known Catholic theologians have criticised it, and concludes that a disputed teaching imposes no obligation. What distinctions resolve the case?
questions.answer: Identify the act: authoritative papal teaching rather than an infallible definition, so it calls for serious assent while remaining the subject of argument; a theologian's criticism is an argument inside the Catholic conversation and does not by itself make the teaching optional for a learner.
questions.distractor: Any criticism by a theologian suspends the teaching, so a student may treat the encyclical's rejected positions as equally available options.
questions.correction: The categories from the first lesson do their work here: not everything is a definition, and not everything non-definitional is optional. Donum Veritatis 23 describes religious submission toward teaching that is not definitive, and 24 allows for legitimate criticism of prudential judgments — which is not the same as declaring a moral teaching void.

questions.prompt: A speaker says the canonisation of a saint adds a new article to the deposit of faith and proves that revelation continues in the Church today. A listener asks how canonisation should be classified and what this implies about the deposit.
questions.answer: Canonisation is a definitive judgment of fact about a person's state, listed among what the doctrinal commentary calls dogmatic facts; it does not add to the deposit of faith, which is held to be complete with the apostolic age.
questions.distractor: Canonisation is a new revelation, which is why the Church can canonise saints in every century.
questions.correction: The second category of teaching covers truths connected with revelation that are not themselves revealed propositions, and the doctrinal commentary names canonisations among its own examples. The Church's ability to act definitively about a person is not evidence of continuing public revelation — an inference the catechism of doctrine and the conciliar account of development both exclude.

questions.prompt: A leaflet defends soliciting money before a devotional image by citing the Council of Trent's decree on the veneration of images. Explain what the decree actually teaches and how a corrected leaflet would read.
questions.answer: The decree teaches that honour shown to images is referred to what they represent, and that no divinity or virtue is believed to be in them on account of which they are to be worshipped or from which anything is to be asked; a corrected leaflet would direct honour to God and ask for prayer.
questions.distractor: The decree permits asking benefits of images provided the intention is religious and the proceeds are used well.
questions.correction: The decree's structure is doxological: honour passes through the sign to the prototype, which is why the same session can say that in venerating images we adore Christ and venerate the saints. Asking anything of an object inverts that structure. The original text is short enough to read in full, which is the practical remedy for misquotation.

questions.prompt: A hospital chaplain faces three requests on one afternoon: a conditional Baptism for a patient whose earlier Baptism used an unclear formula, the anointing of a patient with a chronic but stable illness, and a request to give general absolution to a large group without individual confession. Classify each and state what kind of reasoning answers it.
questions.answer: The first is an evidentiary question about validity settled by investigating form, matter, and intention; the second concerns the proper use of a sacrament intended for the seriously ill and is answered from current norms and pastoral guidance; the third is a question of lawfulness with strict conditions that must be checked in current legislation.
questions.distractor: All three are doctrinal questions that only a bishop's definition could settle, so the chaplain should refuse all three pending clarification.
questions.correction: Each request is answered by a different kind of reasoning, which is the classification skill this level teaches. Conflating them either paralysis or improvisation. The doctrinal content is real in all three — the character doctrine, the sacrament of the sick, the requirement of confession by divine right — but doctrine does not by itself answer questions about evidence and law.

questions.prompt: A devotional article states that Mary dispenses graces at her own discretion and that the saints, being closer to God than we are, answer prayers by their own power. Rewrite the two claims within the Church's teaching using the sources of this level.
questions.answer: Mary's mediation is a participation in Christ's mediation that neither adds to nor subtracts from it, and the saints pray to God for people rather than answering prayers by an independent power of their own.
questions.distractor: Mary's closeness to God gives her a delegated omnipotence, and the saints' power to answer prayers is the reason their invocation is encouraged.
questions.correction: Lumen Gentium 62 attaches an express limitation to the title Mediatrix, and Trent's twenty-fifth session grounds the practice in the saints' own prayers offered through Christ, who alone is Redeemer and Saviour. The rewritten claims keep the practice and remove the transfer of power that the sources exclude.

questions.prompt: You are asked to write a one-page briefing on a disputed ecclesial document that mixes a doctrinal claim, an argument that the claim is continuous with earlier teaching, a pastoral application, and a moral judgment about conduct. Set out the sequence of moves a competent briefing would make and the order in which it would make them.
questions.answer: Identify the speaker, genre, addressees and the act the document performs; separate doctrine from application and example; require the earlier and later propositions with the continuity bridge; analyse the moral claim by object, intention, and circumstances with a located source; and mark clearly which conclusions are teaching and which are prudential or disputed.
questions.distractor: Quote the most solemn-sounding sentence in the document, treat it as settled doctrine, and arrange the remaining material as commentary supporting it.
questions.correction: The sequence matters because each move constrains the next. Classification fixes the weight; the reading method fixes what stratum is being quoted; the development test fixes whether the continuity claim has been argued; and the moral analysis keeps the verdict on actual conduct inside its proper limits. A briefing that starts from the conclusion loses every one of those constraints.
